passage:
Group chat, 9:40 p.m. Someone has posted Himani's class photo with a cartoon nose drawn on it, and the laughing replies keep coming.
Rafiq: Take it down. It's not funny and you all know it.
Rafiq (private): Himani, I've reported the post. You okay?
Himani: not really. why did you do that? now they'll start on you too
Rafiq: Let them. I'm not staying quiet while they do this to you.
Himani: I don't even know what to say. thank you. seriously.
Rafiq: You'd do the same for me.
Himani: I would. Anytime you need backup, I'm there. I mean it.
Himani: I'm showing Mummy the screenshots now.
Twenty minutes later Himani's mother sat beside her on the bed, saved every screenshot, told her none of this was her fault, and wrote to the class teacher that same night. Reading Rafiq's messages, she said, 'Keep that boy close.'

qa.q: What did Rafiq do after telling the group to take the photo down?
qa.a: He reported the post and asked Himani if she was okay.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when she wrote 'thank you. seriously'?
qa.a: She felt deeply grateful and a little stunned, and also worried that the others would now start on Rafiq too 🤍

qa.q: How could Himani show her thanks beyond one message?
qa.a: She could tell Rafiq face to face how much it meant, and keep her promise to back him up if he is ever targeted.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see the moment he spoke up in the group chat?
qa.a: He seems to see it as simply what a friend does, even knowing the others might turn on him next.

grounding: Shows a teen mocked online who feels deeply grateful when a friend stands by her, thanks him and promises support in return.

passage: The video had reached half of Kolur by evening: Rekha slipping in the mud outside the temple, her basket of marigolds flying, a boy's voice laughing over it. On the chat app, the kasba school group filled with laughing faces and nicknames. Rekha sat on the step of her family's shop, phone face down. Ganga came running from the bus stand with her own phone held up. She had typed in the group, 'Delete this. Rekha is my friend, and anyone laughing at her is laughing at me too.' Two boys had already deleted their comments. Rekha's eyes filled. 'You didn't have to,' she whispered. 'Yes, I did.' Rekha squeezed her hand hard. 'Next time it's you, I'm the first one there.' Then together they showed Amma the video. Amma put down her ledger, hugged Rekha, and phoned the class teacher before closing the shop that night.

qa.q: Where was Rekha sitting when Ganga arrived?
qa.a: She was sitting on the step of her family's shop with her phone face down.

qa.q: How can you tell Rekha felt grateful to Ganga?
qa.a: Her eyes filled, she squeezed Ganga's hand hard and promised to be first there next time, which shows deep gratitude and relief.

qa.q: Which of Rekha's choices helped most after the video spread?
qa.a: Thanking Ganga openly, and then showing Amma so an adult could contact the teacher that same night.

qa.q: How does Ganga see the mocking in the group?
qa.a: She sees it as an attack on her too, so she refuses to stay silent while her friend is laughed at.

grounding: Illustrates a friend's loyalty during online mockery and the target's gratitude and promise of support in return.

passage: Jaya, you think your Masi was always the sensible one? Sit, I'll tell you. I was sixteen, at my friend Pooja's birthday on a rooftop in Pune. Her cousins brought beer and a packet of cigarettes, and soon the whole circle was holding a can. Someone pushed one at me: 'Madhuri, don't be boring.' My stomach dropped. I laughed and said, 'Boring is my speciality, yaar. I'll be the one who remembers your party,' and grabbed a cola instead. A few laughed, one rolled her eyes. When the cigarettes came round, I said I had to call home and went downstairs to wait for my father's scooter. Pooja phoned me the next day to say sorry about her cousins. That's how I learned who my real friends were, Jaya. Pooja is still one of them, and she still teases me about that cola.

qa.q: What did Madhuri take instead of the beer?
qa.a: Madhuri grabbed a cola instead.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when the can was pushed at her?
qa.a: Madhuri felt a jolt of nervous pressure, since the stomach dropped, but stayed steady enough to joke a way out.

qa.q: Which choice at the party helped Madhuri most, and why?
qa.a: The light joke, followed by the exit of waiting downstairs, let Madhuri refuse without a fight and get home safely.

qa.q: How did Pooja see what happened at her party?
qa.a: Pooja seemed sorry about her cousins pushing drinks, because she phoned the next day to apologise and stayed a real friend.

grounding: An elder's story of refusing drinks and cigarettes at a party with a joke and an exit, and a real friend respecting that choice.

passage: The vape went round the sofa at Asif's cousin's flat, sweet mango smoke hanging under the fan. 'Come on, Sonali, one pull. Don't be the boring one,' said a girl from the hockey team. Sonali's phone showed four percent, and her mother wasn't due to pick her up for an hour. Leaving outright wasn't simple. She smiled. 'My lungs are for the hockey final, sorry, not for mangoes.' A couple of people laughed; the girl shrugged. When the vape came round again, Sonali stood up, said she needed air, and went out to the balcony. Asif followed with his charger. 'Plug in here,' he said. 'And ignore them. You said no, that's the end of it.' She charged her phone, texted her mother to come early, and waited on the balcony with Asif, talking about the final, until the car pulled up below.

qa.q: What reason did Sonali give for refusing the vape?
qa.a: She joked that her lungs were for the hockey final, not for mangoes.

qa.q: Why might Sonali have felt uneasy about simply walking out?
qa.a: She was anxious because her phone was almost dead and her mother wasn't due for an hour, so she had no easy way home.

qa.q: What small step helped Sonali handle the pressure the second time?
qa.a: She took a break on the balcony, charged her phone and texted her mother to come early.

qa.q: How does Asif see Sonali's refusal?
qa.a: He respects it as final and backs her up with a charger and company, the way a real friend would 👍

grounding: Shows a teen refusing a vape at a party with a joke and an exit despite a dying phone, and a friend respecting the no.

passage: All week the girls at the bus stop in Kuttanad talked about the toddy shop behind the paddy fields: who had sneaked a sip at the harvest festival, who had gone red and giggly. Gopika laughed along, but at night she kept wondering what it tasted like, and what it felt like to be one of the ones with a story. On Sunday she helped her cousin Ankita, home from nursing college, dry chillies on the terrace. 'Chechi, is one sip really so bad?' Ankita didn't scold. She explained that alcohol hits a brain that is still growing harder, affecting memory and judgement, and that starting young makes it easier to keep going. Gopika turned a chilli over slowly. 'I think I mostly want to be part of the bus-stop talk,' she admitted. 'Then you already know what you're choosing,' Ankita said. Gopika decided she didn't need the sip.

qa.q: What were the girls at the bus stop talking about all week?
qa.a: The toddy shop behind the paddy fields, and who had sneaked a sip at the harvest festival.

qa.q: What does Gopika's admission on the terrace suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She felt curious and a little left out, wanting to belong to the bus-stop talk more than wanting the drink itself.

qa.q: What helped Gopika make her choice?
qa.a: Asking Ankita honestly and hearing real effects on a growing brain let her choose with facts instead of image.

qa.q: How does Ankita see Gopika's question?
qa.a: She sees it as honest curiosity to answer calmly, not something to scold, so she explains and lets Gopika decide.

grounding: Shows a teen noticing that her curiosity about alcohol is about image, learning its effects on a growing brain and choosing knowingly.

passage: Coach's log, Thursday, under-16 football. After practice I saw Tejas, the older lad who hangs around the ground, walk Ujjwal to the gate and press something into his hand. Ujjwal handed it straight back, shook his head and walked back towards the pavilion instead of leaving with him. Ten minutes later he found me by the kit bags. He said Tejas had been giving free vapes to a few of the juniors for weeks and had now asked him to 'carry a few packets to school, easy money.' His voice was shaking. I told him he had done exactly the right thing, that none of this was on him, and stayed with him while I rang the school's safeguarding lead, Mrs Fernandes. She came to the ground within the hour, spoke with Ujjwal and called his parents in that evening. We are reporting Tejas's visits to the police and the ground manager.

qa.q: What did Tejas ask Ujjwal to do?
qa.a: He asked him to carry a few packets to school, calling it easy money.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's shaking voice suggest?
qa.a: He was frightened and nervous about reporting an older boy, but determined enough to do it anyway.

qa.q: What did the coach's response get right?
qa.a: The coach said it was not Ujjwal's fault, stayed with him and brought in the safeguarding lead the same day.

qa.q: How might Tejas see the free vapes he handed out?
qa.a: He likely sees them as bait to pull juniors into his circle and get them carrying packets for him.

grounding: A coach's note showing a teen recognise an older lad's free vapes as a hook, refuse, leave and tell a trusted adult.

passage: Tuesday night. Diary, today was weird. Ramesh from Class 12 stopped me near the cycle stand and held out a strip of pills and a box of sweets. 'Free, Tushar. Makes exam stress vanish. Come sit with us at lunch.' Then he said if I liked them, I could sell a few to the Class 9 kids and keep some for myself. That's when my stomach went cold. Nobody gives stuff away free. It's a hook, to get me owing him. I said, 'No thanks, I'm late for tuition,' and cycled off fast. At dinner I told Papa everything. He put his roti down, said I'd done nothing wrong and he was glad I walked away. He called Principal ma'am right then, and she said she will speak to the school counsellor and to Ramesh's parents tomorrow morning. I feel lighter now. Still a bit scared of seeing Ramesh at the stand.

qa.q: What did Ramesh hold out to Tushar near the cycle stand?
qa.a: He held out a strip of pills and a box of sweets.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when Ramesh mentioned selling to the Class 9 kids?
qa.a: Tushar felt a cold jolt of alarm, sensing the free offer was a hook meant to leave Tushar owing Ramesh.

qa.q: What would you advise Tushar to do if Ramesh approaches again?
qa.a: Keep saying no, move towards other people, and tell Papa or the counsellor straight away.

qa.q: How does Papa see what Tushar told him?
qa.a: Papa takes it seriously and is glad Tushar walked away, so he calls the principal that same evening.

grounding: A diary showing a teen recognise an older student's free pills as a hook, refuse, leave and tell a parent the same day.

passage: Payal, you asked why I still run every morning. When I was fifteen, in the hostel at Kalimpong, my Ama-la fell ill back home and I couldn't go to her. Exams were close and I stopped sleeping. One night a senior left a half bottle of rum in the common room, and I sat staring at it, thinking, just one glass and this weight will lift. My hand was already on it. Then I thought of my uncle, who started drinking 'just for sleep' and ended up needing it for everything. I put it back and knocked on the warden's door instead, crying so hard I couldn't talk at first. She made me tea, sat with me, and took me to the school counsellor the next day. The counsellor suggested running before class. I, Dolma, have been running ever since, and I phone a friend when the weight comes back.

qa.q: What did the senior leave in the common room?
qa.a: A senior left a half bottle of rum there.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling while staring at the rum that night?
qa.a: Dolma felt worn down with worry and sleeplessness and hoped one glass would lift that heavy sadness for a while.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Dolma's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Remembering the uncle who drank 'just for sleep' and knocking on the warden's door; it swapped quick relief for real help.

qa.q: How might the warden have seen Dolma that night?
qa.a: The warden likely saw a frightened, worried student who needed comfort first, so offered tea and then the counsellor.

grounding: An elder's story of wanting alcohol to ease stress, seeing that quick relief can deepen the problem, and turning to a warden, a counsellor and running.

passage: Rain had drummed on the tin roof for three days, the football ground was a lake, and the notice on the counsellor's door said 'On leave till Monday'. Pankaj's board results were due Friday and his chest felt tight all the time. In his uncle's cupboard there was a packet of cigarettes, and he kept thinking about it. Everyone said they calm you down. On Wednesday night he actually took the packet out and stood by the window with it. Then he remembered his uncle coughing every morning, saying he had only started because of exams. Pankaj put it back and knocked on his sister's door. Bidisha pulled out an earphone. 'Can't sleep?' He told her everything. She didn't laugh. She handed him one earbud, played the tabla recordings he used to practise to, and said, 'Tomorrow we go to Ma together, and Monday to the counsellor.' He slept properly for the first time that week.

qa.q: What did the notice on the counsellor's door say?
qa.a: It said 'On leave till Monday'.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling as he stood by the window with the packet?
qa.a: He was tense and anxious about his results, tempted by the idea that cigarettes would calm him, and torn about using them.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Pankaj, and why?
qa.a: Talking to Bidisha instead of smoking; she gave him music, company and a plan to see Ma and the counsellor.

qa.q: How does Bidisha see her brother's late-night knock?
qa.a: She sees he is struggling and treats it seriously, offering music and company rather than laughing.

grounding: Shows a teen tempted to use cigarettes to ease stress who instead talks to his sister and turns to music and a counsellor.

passage: Since Pongal, Chaitanya had been missing the morning bus more and more. In Kottur everyone knew he sat with the older boys behind the rice mill in the evenings, and Sarika had smelt arrack on his shirt twice. Today he came to class with a cut on his chin and couldn't remember how he'd fallen off his cycle. At lunch, under the neem tree, Sarika didn't list his mistakes. 'I miss the Chaitanya who beat me at kabaddi,' she said quietly. 'I'm scared you'll get really hurt. Will you talk to someone?' He looked at the ground and said he couldn't stop now. After school she went straight to Selvi teacher and told her about the fall and the arrack. Selvi teacher thanked her, said she had done the right thing, and walked to Chaitanya's house with the headmaster that same evening to speak to his mother.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya come to class with today?
qa.a: He came with a cut on his chin and couldn't remember how he'd fallen off his cycle.

qa.q: What does Sarika's quiet line under the neem tree show about her feelings?
qa.a: It shows she felt scared and deeply caring, missing her old friend and worried he'd get badly hurt.

qa.q: Why was telling Selvi teacher the right next step for Sarika?
qa.a: Chaitanya was getting hurt and said he couldn't stop, so his safety was at risk and an adult needed to act.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya seem to take Sarika's words?
qa.a: He seems both cared for and ashamed, which is why he looked at the ground and admitted he couldn't stop.

grounding: Shows a teen expressing care without lecturing to a friend whose drinking is getting worse and telling a teacher once his safety is at risk.

passage: In Kraków, the tram stop outside the skate park was where Lucia usually met Marek, but lately he was late, red-eyed and quiet. He smoked weed most afternoons now, then most mornings too. His football boots had stayed in his locker for a month. On Friday night he swayed by his scooter, fumbling for the key, and said he'd ride home. Lucia's heart hammered. She didn't lecture. 'I'm not judging you. I just want you home in one piece, and I'm worried about how much you need it lately. Will you see the school counsellor, Mr Nowak, with me on Monday?' He shrugged, but let her hold the key. Then she called her mum. Her mum drove over in ten minutes, took them both home, and sat in the kitchen with Marek's parents that same night while he slept upstairs.

qa.q: Where did Lucia usually meet Marek?
qa.a: At the tram stop outside the skate park.

qa.q: What was Lucia feeling when Marek fumbled for his scooter key?
qa.a: Her heart hammered because she was frightened he'd get hurt, yet she stayed calm and caring instead of angry.

qa.q: What went right in how Lucia handled that night?
qa.a: She spoke with care, suggested the counsellor, kept him off the scooter and called her mum at once because his safety was at risk.

qa.q: What would change if Lucia had lectured Marek instead?
qa.a: He might have got defensive and refused to hand over the key, leaving him to ride home unsafe.

grounding: Shows a teen caring for a friend whose weed use is worsening without lecturing, encouraging help and getting an adult when his safety is at risk.

passage: Before Ritu left for her cousin's wedding in the next village, Papa had tapped her phone. 'Anything feels wrong, you call me. Any hour. I come, no questions tonight. We talk tomorrow, if you want.' By midnight the baraat had turned loud. Some of the boys were passing a bottle behind the tent, and one of them, swaying, offered Ritu and her friend Damini a ride home on his motorcycle. Damini whispered, 'Your papa will be so angry you're still here.' Ritu hesitated, then remembered his words. She stepped behind the generator and called. 'Papa, can you come?' Twenty minutes later his tractor headlights appeared on the mud road. He wrapped his shawl round both girls, dropped Damini home first, and asked nothing all the way. In the morning, over tea, Ritu told him everything herself.

qa.q: How did Papa arrive to pick up Ritu?
qa.a: His tractor headlights appeared on the mud road twenty minutes after she called.

qa.q: Why did Ritu hesitate before calling Papa?
qa.a: She felt worried and a little embarrassed that he'd be angry she was still out at midnight, until she remembered his promise.

qa.q: What could Damini learn from how Ritu handled the ride offer?
qa.a: That using a parent's safe-call offer beats getting on a motorcycle with someone who's been drinking; safety first, talking later 👍

qa.q: How does Papa see Ritu's midnight call?
qa.a: He sees it as her trusting him, so he keeps his promise to ask nothing that night.

grounding: Shows a teen using her parent's no-questions safe-call offer to leave an unsafe situation, with talking left for the next day.

passage: Kwame had rolled his eyes when Mum said it in the hallway: 'Any time you're somewhere unsafe, ring me. I'll come, and I won't ask a single question tonight.' At Nour's older brother's flat in Leeds, the party changed after eleven. Strangers arrived, someone tipped white pills onto the kitchen counter, and a man blocked the balcony door, laughing too loudly. Kwame's palms went damp. He texted Nour, stuck across the room: 'I'm leaving. Come with?' She nodded and slipped out behind him. On the stairwell he rang Mum. She answered on the second ring. 'Corner by the bus shelter, ten minutes,' she said, and kept her word: no lecture, just the heater on and a packet of biscuits on the seat. She dropped Nour at her door first. At breakfast Kwame started talking without being asked, and Mum just listened.

qa.q: What was waiting on the car seat when Mum picked Kwame up?
qa.a: A packet of biscuits, and the heater was on.

qa.q: What do Kwame's damp palms suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he felt uneasy and frightened as the party turned unsafe with strangers and pills.

qa.q: What would you advise a friend in Kwame's place?
qa.a: Leave with a friend, call the parent who offered a safe ride, and save the talk for the next day.

qa.q: How might Mum see the call from the stairwell?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved he trusted her, which is why she kept her promise of no lecture that night ❤️

grounding: Shows a teen using his mother's promise of a no-questions pickup to leave an unsafe party, with the talk saved for the morning.

passage: At the Dussehra mela in Sirsa, behind the giant wheel, Raghav had taken two drags of a bidi the older boys passed round. He coughed, they laughed, and he laughed too. Now, two days later, he couldn't look at his mother at meals. He scrubbed his hands at the handpump twice before sleeping, as if the smell were still there. On Sunday Vandana Bua came to visit, and he found himself walking with her to the fields. 'Bua, I did something stupid,' he blurted, and told her. She was quiet a moment, then squeezed his shoulder. 'One stupid thing at a mela doesn't make you a bad boy, Raghav. What matters is what you decide now.' Together they worked it out: no more going behind the wheel with those boys, and he would tell his mother himself that evening. He did, and she hugged him.

qa.q: Where did Raghav take the drags of the bidi?
qa.a: Behind the giant wheel at the Dussehra mela in Sirsa.

qa.q: Why couldn't Raghav look at his mother at meals?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and guilty about the bidi, as if everyone could still sense it on him.

qa.q: Which limit did Raghav set, and why does it help?
qa.a: He decided not to go behind the wheel with those boys again, which removes the situation where he felt pushed.

qa.q: How does Vandana Bua see Raghav's confession?
qa.a: She sees one mistake, not a bad boy, and turns his attention to what he chooses next.

grounding: Shows a teen ashamed after trying a bidi once, learning one mistake does not define him, being honest with trusted adults and setting a clear limit.

passage: Gabriel had been lying awake since Saturday. At Lars's family cabin outside Bergen, with the grown-ups asleep, Lars had pulled a bottle of vodka from under a bunk. Gabriel drank three quick shots to keep up, then spent the night being sick in the snow while Lars held his jacket. Now every time his father smiled at him, he felt like a liar. By Tuesday he couldn't stand it. In the car after swim practice he said, 'Dad, I need to tell you something, and I'm really ashamed.' His father listened without interrupting, then pulled over. 'Thank you for telling me. One bad night doesn't make you who you are. Let's talk about what you'll do next time.' Gabriel said he would text his dad for a ride if bottles came out again, and he wouldn't play drinking games at all. His father nodded. 'That's a good line to draw.'

qa.q: Where did Gabriel drink the vodka?
qa.a: At Lars's family cabin outside Bergen, with the grown-ups asleep.

qa.q: What was Gabriel feeling each time his father smiled at him?
qa.a: He felt guilty and ashamed, like a liar hiding something.

qa.q: What makes Gabriel's plan for next time a good one?
qa.a: It is clear and practical: text his dad for a ride if bottles come out, and no drinking games at all.

qa.q: How does Gabriel's father see the confession?
qa.a: He is grateful Gabriel was honest and treats it as one bad night to learn from, not a verdict on his son 🤍

grounding: Shows a teen who feels ashamed after drinking once, is honest with his father, learns one mistake does not define him and sets clear limits.

passage: Monday. After Mama Ji laughed at the wedding, 'Siddharth, you're thin as a broom,' Siddharth scrolled gym reels until midnight: perfect arms, shining abs. He wore two T-shirts to school the next day so nobody would see his shoulders. Thursday. His cousin Disha caught him frowning at his phone. She opened a photo editor and, in three swipes, made her own arms bigger and her waist smaller. 'Half those reels are lit, posed and edited like this,' she said. 'You're comparing yourself to a filter.' He stared at the screen for a long time. Two weeks later. Siddharth had joined the school swimming batch. Tired and dripping after his first full length without stopping, he caught sight of himself in the changing-room mirror and, for once, thought about what his shoulders had just done, not how they looked.

qa.q: What did Disha show Siddharth with the photo editor?
qa.a: In three swipes she made her own arms bigger and her waist smaller.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth wear two T-shirts to school?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and self-conscious about his thin shoulders after Mama Ji's joke and the reels.

qa.q: What helped Siddharth start to shift how he saw his body?
qa.a: Seeing how reels are edited, then swimming, which let him notice what his body can do rather than how it looks 💪

qa.q: How does Disha see Siddharth's scrolling?
qa.a: She sees him comparing himself to edited images, so she shows him the trick instead of just telling him he's fine.

grounding: Shows a teen ashamed of his body after a comment and online pictures, noticing the standard is edited and shifting focus to what his body does.

passage: Ritu, you think I didn't care about mirrors at your age? I was fourteen when my aunties started, at every function: 'Nirmala is getting so dark, so round, who will marry her?' The film posters outside Lakshmi Talkies showed heroines with skin like milk and waists like pencils, and I hated my arms, my face, everything. I stopped going to kho-kho practice so nobody would see me run. Then I got a holiday job at Venkat uncle's photo studio. One afternoon he showed me a heroine's photo before and after his brush: he lightened her skin, shaved her waist, erased a scar. 'Nobody looks like this, child. Not even her.' I went back to kho-kho that week. Those legs made me captain two years later. So when you tell me your photos online look wrong, listen to Nirmala Paati: ask what your body can do.

qa.q: What did Venkat uncle change in the heroine's photo?
qa.a: He lightened her skin, shaved her waist and erased a scar.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when the aunties commented at functions?
qa.a: Nirmala felt ashamed and hurt, hating every part of that body, enough to quit kho-kho so nobody would watch.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Nirmala's choice?
qa.a: Seeing the before-and-after photo at the studio showed the posters were edited, so going back to kho-kho made sense.

qa.q: How did Venkat uncle see the heroine's poster?
qa.a: He knew it was his own brushwork, not a real person, and wanted Nirmala to know nobody looks like that.

grounding: An elder's story of body shame from comments and retouched pictures, learning the standard was edited and focusing on what the body can do.

passage: It started in Class 9, when I was still the shortest in our section. 'Oye, Shankar, stand on the bench so we can see you!' Every morning someone had a new line, and every morning I laughed along or snapped back, which only gave them more to play with. Looking back, the change came from something small. One day I just didn't react. I kept copying the board. It went quiet faster than I expected. But two of them kept going, leaving a toy ladder on my desk every day for a week, so I finally told Sangeeta Ma'am after chemistry. She listened, said it was not my fault, moved those two to the front bench that same afternoon and called their parents. What I remember most is what she said at the door: 'Your worth isn't decided by a class vote, Shankar.' I'm still short. I've stopped thinking that's a problem.

qa.q: What did two classmates leave on Shankar's desk?
qa.a: They left a toy ladder on the desk every day for a week.

qa.q: What was Shankar probably feeling while laughing along every morning?
qa.a: Shankar laughed along or snapped back every morning, which suggests feeling hurt and embarrassed while trying to hide it.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Not reacting took the fun away for most of them, and telling Sangeeta Ma'am when it kept going got an adult to stop it.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta Ma'am see the teasing?
qa.a: She sees it as repeated mockery that needs action, not a joke, so she moves the two and calls their parents.

grounding: A first-person look back at being mocked for height, learning not to feed it, telling a teacher when it repeated, and that worth is not decided by others.

passage: PE teacher's note, 14 August. During warm-up I heard Shalini's group call Bhavna 'pimple map' again while she tied her laces. This is the third time this month I've heard something about her skin or her weight. Bhavna didn't turn round. She finished her laces, jogged to the front and kept her eyes on the cones, though her ears had gone red. After class she came to me with a friend and asked, very quietly, if I could make it stop, because it happens in the corridor too. I thanked her for telling me and said none of it had anything to do with her worth. I spoke to Shalini's group before the next bell, recorded it, and passed it to the class teacher, Mr D'Souza, who phoned their parents that afternoon. I will keep a close eye on warm-ups and corridors.

qa.q: What did Shalini's group call Bhavna?
qa.a: They called her 'pimple map' during warm-up.

qa.q: What do Bhavna's red ears suggest while she kept her eyes on the cones?
qa.a: They suggest she felt embarrassed and hurt, even though she chose not to react.

qa.q: What made Bhavna's approach effective?
qa.a: She didn't feed the jokes in the moment, then told a teacher once it kept happening, so an adult could stop it.

qa.q: How might Shalini's group see the joke?
qa.a: They may treat it as harmless fun, not noticing how it hurts Bhavna or that it says more about them than her.

grounding: A teacher's note showing a teen mocked about her skin and weight who ignores it, avoids feeding it and tells a teacher when it repeats.
